about: AEC Tech Radar: a research map of construction (AEC) technology firms. Entries marked verification: ai-draft were researched by an AI and not yet checked by a person; check the sources before relying on them.

categories.name: Project data platforms
categories.question: Where does all project data live, and can AI reach it?
categories.body:
The systems of record for drawings, models, RFIs (requests for information),
submittals, costs and site logs. Most large firms already run one or more.

**Why it matters for an AI-native firm:** AI can only reason over data it can
reach. A firm whose project history sits in clean, connected platforms can
train, search and automate across every project; one whose data sits in email
and shared drives can't. In 2025–26 the big platforms (Procore, Autodesk,
Bentley, Nemetschek) all added AI assistants and "agents" (AI that carries out
multi-step tasks) on top of the data they hold, so choosing a platform is now
also choosing an AI strategy.

**What to ask a client:** how many systems hold project data, who owns the
data contractually, and whether it can be exported in open formats.

categories.name: Document and contract intelligence
categories.question: Can AI read, check and answer questions about the project's documents?
categories.body:
AI that reads drawings, specifications, contracts, RFIs and submittals:
answering questions, flagging risky clauses, checking submittals against the
spec, and spotting changes between drawing revisions.

**Why it matters for an AI-native firm:** construction runs on documents, and
most of the knowledge a site team needs is buried in them. This is where large
language models (the technology behind ChatGPT and Claude) fit most naturally,
so it is one of the fastest-moving categories. It is also consolidating fast:
platforms are building or buying these features (for example Trimble agreeing
to buy Document Crunch in 2026).

**Watch for:** answers without citations, and who is accountable when an AI
misses a clause.

categories.name: Design and feasibility automation
categories.question: Can AI generate and test design options faster than people can?
categories.body:
"Generative design" tools: software that produces many layout or massing
options from rules and goals (site, unit mix, parking, cost) so people can
compare them, plus AI assistants inside design software.

**Why it matters for an AI-native firm:** it moves effort from drawing options
to choosing between them, and lets a contractor or developer test feasibility
before paying for full design. For design-and-build firms it can connect
design choices to cost and programme early.

**Watch for:** options that look good but ignore local planning rules, and
how outputs move into the firm's main design tools (Revit and others).

categories.name: Carbon and sustainability analysis
categories.question: Can the firm measure and cut the carbon in what it designs and builds?
categories.body:
Tools for life-cycle assessment (LCA: the environmental impact of a building
from materials to demolition), embodied carbon, environmental product
declarations (EPDs: standard statements of a product's impact) and regulatory
reporting.

**Why it matters for an AI-native firm:** carbon reporting is increasingly a
regulatory and client requirement, and it depends on detailed material data,
which is exactly what AI can help gather and keep up to date. Firms that link
their design models to carbon data can compare options on carbon as easily as
on cost.

categories.name: Preconstruction and estimating
categories.question: Can AI speed up quantity take-off, estimating and bidding?
categories.body:
"Take-off" is measuring quantities (areas, lengths, counts) from drawings to
price a job. AI tools now detect and measure rooms, walls and fittings on
drawings automatically, and help compare subcontractor bids.

**Why it matters for an AI-native firm:** estimating is repetitive, deadline-
driven and decides which jobs a firm wins and whether they make money. Faster
take-off means more bids, or more time spent on judgement rather than
measurement.

**Watch for:** accuracy claims are almost always the vendor's own; ask for
trials on the firm's own past drawings.

categories.name: Planning, scheduling and risk forecasting
categories.question: Can AI build better programmes and predict delays before they happen?
categories.body:
Two different approaches: **optimisation** (software that generates and
compares many possible construction sequences) and **forecasting** (machine
learning trained on thousands of past schedules to predict where a programme
will slip).

**Why it matters for an AI-native firm:** delay is the industry's biggest
money-loser. A firm that can test scenarios in hours and price schedule risk
from evidence rather than workshops can bid and manage differently. This is
one of the clearest cases of AI changing a core business decision rather than
just saving admin time.

**Watch for:** forecasting needs lots of historical schedules; ask whose data
the model learned from and whether the firm's own data improves it.

categories.name: Site capture and progress tracking
categories.question: Does the firm know, objectively and weekly, what has actually been built?
categories.body:
Cameras (often 360° cameras on a helmet), drones and laser scanners capture the
site; computer vision (AI that interprets images) maps the images to the plans
and compares what's built against the model and the programme.

**Why it matters for an AI-native firm:** it turns the site into data. Progress,
quality and payment discussions can rest on evidence instead of opinion, and
the captured history becomes training data for better planning. It is a
relatively mature category with many large-contractor deployments.

**Watch for:** the value depends on teams acting on what the system shows, not
just capturing it.

categories.name: Construction robotics and autonomy
categories.question: Which physical site tasks can machines now do reliably?
categories.body:
Robots and autonomy kits for specific, repetitive tasks: marking out layouts
on floors, finishing drywall, driving piles, trenching, drilling. Most are
offered as "robots as a service" (rented per job, with support) rather than
sold.

**Why it matters for an AI-native firm:** labour shortages and safety. Robots
are where AI reaches the physical work, but they succeed task by task, not
as general-purpose site workers, and they need the digital model to be right.

**Watch for:** speed claims are usually from the vendor; ask what the site has
to look like for the robot to work (clear floors, finished slabs, connectivity).

categories.name: Industrialised and offsite construction
categories.question: Can building move from the site to the factory, and is it worth it?
categories.body:
Modular, prefabricated and factory-built components, and the design-for-
manufacture approach (designing so parts can be made in a factory) behind
them.

**Why it matters for an AI-native firm:** factories generate consistent data
and repeatable processes, which suit automation far better than one-off sites.
But this category has a hard history: several heavily funded firms failed,
most visibly Katerra in 2021. Any transformation plan that leans on offsite
needs to show it has learned those lessons.

categories.name: Digital twins and operations
categories.question: Does the asset keep producing useful data after handover?
categories.body:
A "digital twin" is a model of a building or infrastructure asset that is kept
up to date with real data (sensors, inspections, maintenance records), so
owners can monitor, simulate and plan maintenance.

**Why it matters for an AI-native firm:** it extends a contractor's role
beyond handover into long-term services, and closes the loop: data on how
assets actually perform can improve the next design. It is also where the
business-model change (from one-off projects to ongoing services) is most
visible.

**Watch for:** "digital twin" is used loosely in marketing; ask what data
stays live and who keeps it updated.

companies.name: ALICE Technologies
companies.summary: AI that generates and compares thousands of possible construction schedules for large capital projects.
companies.ring_note: Real deployments with large contractors (Parsons, Kajima named by BuiltWorlds), but the value depends on the client having good schedule and model data. Pilot on one live project before committing.

sources.title: ALICE company profile
sources.supports: Menlo Park base; Stanford research origin; customers including Parsons, HDCC and Kajima; founding year (2015 in text, 2013 in key facts)

sources.title: AI-based tool optimizes construction schedules straight from P6
sources.supports: works directly from Oracle Primavera P6 schedules, without a full BIM model; founder Rene Morkos

sources.title: ALICE Optimize product page
sources.supports: imports and exports Primavera P6, Primavera Cloud and Microsoft Project schedules

sources.title: Insights Agent product page
sources.supports: a conversational AI agent for questioning a schedule, citing its sources

companies.body:
## What it does
"Generative scheduling": a planner describes the work, crews and constraints,
and the software generates many feasible schedules and lets the team compare
them (cost, duration, resources). ALICE Pro starts from a BIM model; ALICE
Optimize works on existing Primavera P6 or Microsoft Project schedules. It
markets heavily to industrial work (data centres, energy, mining) as well as
commercial building.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
Scheduling is a core decision, not admin. Being able to test "what if we add a
second crane / change the sequence" in hours changes how a firm bids and
recovers delays. It is one of the clearer examples of AI informing a business
decision rather than saving clerical time.

## Evidence and caveats
- Founding year is inconsistent: BuiltWorlds gives 2015 in its text and 2013
  in its key-facts box, so it's left blank here.
- Customer names come from a directory listing; performance claims on the
  company's pages are its own.

## To check
- Independent case studies with measured savings.
- Current funding and ownership (not researched in this pass).

companies.name: Autodesk
companies.summary: Maker of Revit; its Forma cloud now combines design and construction (the former Autodesk Construction Cloud) with an AI assistant and agents.
companies.ring_note: Most AEC firms already use Autodesk tools, so its AI arrives by default. Treat individual AI features as trial-stage, as several were in beta in 2025–26.

sources.title: Autodesk Construction Cloud becomes Autodesk Forma
sources.supports: Autodesk Construction Cloud is now part of Forma, an industry cloud for design and construction

sources.title: Meet Autodesk Assistant, AI-native intelligence in Forma
sources.supports: Autodesk Assistant answers questions about project records and cites source documents

sources.title: The future is here, Autodesk reveals a unified Forma for design and build
sources.supports: AU 2025 announcements (Forma Building Design, Revit as a connected client); Autodesk says AI offers options and people decide

companies.body:
## What it does
Design software (including Revit) plus Forma, a cloud platform that now spans
early design (Forma Site Design, Forma Building Design), data management
(formerly Autodesk Docs) and construction (the former Autodesk Construction
Cloud). Autodesk Assistant and a growing set of AI agents sit across it.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
For many firms, Autodesk holds the design data that every other AI tool needs.
How open that data is (and on what terms) shapes what the firm can build
itself versus buy from Autodesk.

## Evidence and caveats
- Most evidence here is Autodesk's own announcements; independent reviews of
  the AI features weren't gathered in this pass.
- Headquarters and founding year not checked.

companies.name: Bentley Systems
companies.summary: Infrastructure engineering software built around its iTwin digital-twin platform, adding AI design and assistant tools.
companies.ring_note: A default for infrastructure-heavy firms. Newer AI apps (OpenSite+, SYNCHRO+, Copilot) are individually "trial".

sources.title: Bentley pushes boundaries with infrastructure AI and Cloud Connect
sources.supports: Year in Infrastructure 2025 announcements (Infrastructure Cloud Connect, iTwin Engage, SYNCHRO+, AI search in ProjectWise)

sources.title: Bentley Systems announces generative AI game-changer for civil site design
sources.supports: OpenSite+ uses generative AI for civil site design, built on iTwin

sources.title: iTwin Platform
sources.supports: iTwin as the foundation for software to design, build and operate infrastructure assets

companies.body:
## What it does
Engineering and project-delivery software for infrastructure (products
named in the sources include ProjectWise, SYNCHRO and OpenSite+), with iTwin as a platform for digital twins
that combine engineering models, reality data and sensors. AI features include
generative civil site design, 4D sequencing and an assistant.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
For an infrastructure contractor, the long-term opportunity is operating
assets, not just building them; digital twins are how that data stays live
after handover.

## Evidence and caveats
- Some AI items date from 2023–24; current status not rechecked.
- Headquarters and founding year not checked.

companies.name: Buildots
companies.summary: Helmet-mounted 360° cameras plus computer vision that compare what's built on site against the BIM model and programme.
companies.ring_note: Well funded and widely deployed with large contractors; the category is maturing. Trial on one project, and judge it on whether teams act on the data.

sources.title: Buildots raises $45M to help companies track construction progress
sources.supports: $45m raise in May 2025 to cover more stages of the construction life cycle

sources.title: Israeli AI construction startup Buildots raises $130 million
sources.supports: founded 2018 by Roy Danon, Aviv Leibovici and Yakir Sudry; a $130m round taking total funding to $297m (date not confirmed in this pass)

sources.title: Construction Intelligence Platform
sources.supports: captures by 360° camera, drone or laser scan, compared with BIM and schedule

companies.body:
## What it does
Site teams walk the site with a 360° camera on a helmet (or use drones or
scans). Computer vision works out what has been installed, element by element,
and compares it with the BIM model and the programme, producing progress
tracking and early warning of delays. The company says captures are processed
within 24–36 hours and that it now covers groundworks to fit-out.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
It turns "how far along are we?" from an opinion into data, every week, across
every project. That data feeds planning, payments and future forecasting.

## Evidence and caveats
- Delay-reduction figures ("up to 50%") are the company's own.
- Two funding reports (May 2025 $45m; a later $130m) are both cited; how they
  relate wasn't confirmed.

## To check
- Date of the $130m round; independent customer outcomes.

companies.name: Built Robotics
companies.summary: Autonomy kits that turn excavators into robots, now focused on utility-scale solar piling (RPD 35) and trenching.
companies.ring_note: Real deployments (over 2GW of solar, per trade press) but a narrow focus on solar in the US and Australia. Relevant for firms doing solar or large earthworks; otherwise a signal of where site autonomy is heading.

sources.title: Robotic solar pile driver three times faster than humans
sources.supports: RPD 35 launch (2023), combining survey, pile distribution, driving and inspection; over 2GW of solar installed with its robots

sources.title: Solar piling
sources.supports: currently deploying in the US and Australia only; robot-as-a-service model

sources.title: Built Robotics technology
sources.supports: 8-layer safety system; cameras that stop the robot when a person comes near

companies.body:
## What it does
Retrofits standard heavy equipment with sensors and software so it can work
autonomously. Its RPD 35 robot surveys, distributes and drives piles for solar
farms; its Exosystem kit enables autonomous trenching. Rented as a service.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
Shows the pattern for site autonomy: narrow, repetitive, well-defined tasks on
open sites first. It also partners with the International Union of Operating
Engineers on training, a model for handling workforce concerns.

## Evidence and caveats
- Speed claims (up to 5× faster) are the company's. Some company pages are
  several years old, so current focus should be confirmed.

companies.name: Canvas
companies.summary: A semi-autonomous robot that sprays and sands drywall to a high finish, operated by trained union workers.
companies.ring_note: Proven on US commercial interiors and backed by Suffolk; Hilti now makes the machines. Relevance depends on the client self-performing finishes.

sources.title: Canvas raises $24M Series B for drywall finishing robot
sources.supports: $24m Series B (2021) led by Menlo Ventures with Suffolk Construction; San Francisco

sources.title: Drywall finishing robot saves time, prevents injuries
sources.supports: semi-autonomous system with a human in the loop

sources.title: Robotics startup Canvas secures $24 million funding
sources.supports: founded 2017 within Otherlab; cumulative funding about $43m (2021)

sources.title: Canvas launches the 1200CX
sources.supports: compact 1200CX robot; Hilti to produce Canvas machines

companies.body:
## What it does
The robot maps the room with lidar and 3D sensing, then sprays and sands
joint compound; people tape and do corners and touch-ups. Canvas works as a
subcontractor, training and employing union finishers to run it.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
A good example of robotics changing a trade's business model (a tech company
acting as subcontractor), not just its tools.

## Evidence and caveats
- Founded 2017 inside Otherlab (trade press; total funding about $43m as of
  2021). No later funding news found.
- Time savings (5–7 days down to about 2) are the company's claims.

companies.name: Document Crunch
companies.summary: AI that reviews construction contracts for risk and helps site teams follow them; Trimble agreed to buy it in April 2026.
companies.ring_note: Proven niche (contract risk) with contractor and insurer use. The Trimble deal makes it likely to become part of Trimble's platform, which matters if the client isn't a Trimble user.

sources.title: Trimble to acquire Document Crunch
sources.supports: Trimble agreed to acquire it (announced 2 April 2026), expected to close in Q2 2026; terms not disclosed

sources.title: Armed with $21.5 million Series B, Document Crunch is ready to grow
sources.supports: $21.5m Series B (October 2024) led by Titanium Ventures with Nemetschek; moved from Florida to Atlanta in 2021; CEO Josh Levy, a construction lawyer

sources.title: Document Crunch raises $9 million
sources.supports: $9m Series A (February 2024) led by Navitas Capital

companies.body:
## What it does
Reads construction contracts and flags risky or unusual clauses (payment,
indemnity, notice periods), then helps project teams find and follow the
obligations during the job. It has added conversational AI and a Microsoft
Word add-in.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
Contract risk is where small misses cost a lot. AI that reads every contract
the same way, every time, and puts obligations in front of site teams is a
clear case of AI reducing commercial risk.

## Evidence and caveats
- Founding year (2019) is from a directory listing only.
- Whether the Trimble acquisition has closed wasn't confirmed in this pass.

## To check
- Acquisition status, and whether it stays available outside Trimble's products.

companies.name: Dusty Robotics
companies.summary: A mobile robot (FieldPrinter) that prints the BIM layout directly onto the floor of a building site.
companies.ring_note: One of the most practical site robots, with case studies from Turner, Skanska and Mortenson (company-published). Easy to trial on a fit-out-heavy project.

sources.title: Dusty Robotics to use $45M in Series B funding to scale digital floorplan printing
sources.supports: $45m Series B (May 2022) led by Scale Venture Partners; total $68.7m

sources.title: Dusty Robotics raises $5M in seed funding
sources.supports: founded 2018 by Tessa Lau and Philipp Herget

sources.title: Dusty Robotics press
sources.supports: FieldPrinter 2 and FieldPrint platform generally available (October 2024)

companies.body:
## What it does
Instead of crews measuring and chalking lines, the robot reads the BIM model
and prints the layout (walls, openings, services) on the slab, to a stated
1/16-inch accuracy. Offered as a service priced by project size.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
It's a direct bridge from the digital model to the physical site: if the model
is right, the layout is right. That rewards firms whose models are accurate,
which is part of the AI-native story.

## Evidence and caveats
- Customer results (e.g. Skanska: 50% faster layout) are company case studies.
- No funding news after 2022 found; current funding not checked.

companies.name: Katerra
companies.summary: A SoftBank-backed attempt to vertically integrate design, manufacturing and construction; went bankrupt in 2021. Kept here as a lesson.
companies.ring_note: Not a vendor. Included because any "transform the whole business model" plan will be compared with Katerra; know why it failed.

sources.title: Katerra files for bankruptcy, seeks to reorganize US operations
sources.supports: 2021 bankruptcy filing

sources.title: What does Katerra's demise mean for the contech and modular industries?
sources.supports: industry reaction and lessons

sources.title: Softbank-backed Katerra's collapse is a failure of pattern-matching
sources.supports: argument that a tech-industry playbook was applied to construction

sources.title: Katerra's $2 billion legacy
sources.supports: overview of what the company tried and spent

companies.body:
## What happened
Katerra tried to own the whole chain: design, its own factories for building
components, and construction. It raised very large sums, made many
acquisitions and took on fixed-price contracts. It filed for bankruptcy in
2021 after cost overruns and losses; its own filing also blamed the pandemic
and losing access to construction bonding after its lender (Greensill)
collapsed.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
It is the obvious cautionary tale for any "transform the whole business"
strategy. Commentators broadly agree on overreach (too many initiatives at
once), weak execution and unprofitable project economics; they disagree on how
much the financing shocks were the cause versus the trigger.

## The lesson for advice
Transform in stages that each pay back; don't buy the whole supply chain
before the core process works; and keep the economics of each project visible.
(This lesson is the researcher's synthesis, not a quote from the sources.)

companies.name: Nemetschek Group
companies.summary: AEC software group (products include Archicad and Allplan) adding a shared AI layer and AI assistant across its products.
companies.ring_note: Products are mature; the cross-brand AI layer is new (first agent shown January 2025, availability from autumn 2025). Also an investor in Document Crunch.

sources.title: Nemetschek to add AI layer to key solutions
sources.supports: October 2024 plan for an AI layer across major products from 2025

sources.title: Nemetschek Group unveils AI assistant integration into Allplan and Archicad
sources.supports: AI Assistant shown at BAU 2025, the group's first agent-based technology

companies.body:
## What it does
A group of design, engineering and construction software brands, including
Archicad and Allplan. Since 2024 it has been building one AI layer that all its products
share, starting with an AI assistant in Archicad and Allplan.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
For firms on Archicad or Allplan, this is the AI that will
arrive inside tools they already use; worth comparing with Autodesk's
approach.

## Evidence and caveats
- Only Archicad and Allplan are confirmed by the sources here; check the full
  brand list on Nemetschek's site. Headquarters and founding year not checked.

companies.name: nPlan
companies.summary: Forecasts schedule delay risk with machine learning trained on hundreds of thousands of past project schedules.
companies.ring_note: Used by major contractors and on UK rail work (BAM partnership; Transpennine Route Upgrade case study, both company-published). Strong fit for large programmes; trial on a live project and compare against the firm's usual risk process.

sources.title: nPlan Limited
sources.supports: founded 2017, based in London; forecasts schedule outcomes and delay risk on megaprojects

sources.title: Construction planning software startup nPlan secures funding from Google Ventures
sources.supports: an $18.5m round led by GV (formerly Google Ventures)

sources.title: BAM joins forces with nPlan on portfolio risk management
sources.supports: partnership with contractor BAM on AI-based portfolio risk management

sources.title: Insights Pro product page
sources.supports: risk analysis in hours without quantification workshops; Power BI and Tableau integration

companies.body:
## What it does
Instead of risk workshops where experts guess how long activities might slip,
nPlan's models learn from a large archive of historical schedules (the company
cites more than 750,000) and give a probabilistic forecast for each activity,
rolled up into a project view of delay risk.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
It replaces expert opinion with evidence from past projects, which is the
heart of the "AI at the centre" idea: decisions grounded in the firm's (and
the industry's) data. It also shows the value of a firm keeping its own
schedule history.

## Evidence and caveats
- Funding totals differ between databases (Dealroom about $36.5m, CB Insights
  about $34.4m), so no total is given here.
- The schedule-count and speed claims are the company's own.

## To check
- Whether a client's own schedules improve the model, and who owns that data.

companies.name: One Click LCA
companies.summary: Life-cycle assessment and embodied-carbon software for buildings, infrastructure and building products.
companies.ring_note: A long-established tool for carbon reporting, regularly updated (monthly 2026 releases, including an AI agent for importing bills of materials).

sources.title: Finland's One Click LCA secures €40m growth investment
sources.supports: €40m from PSG Equity and InfraVia Capital Partners (November 2023)

sources.title: One Click LCA company profile
sources.supports: founded 2001; Helsinki headquarters

sources.title: What's new in One Click LCA in August 2026
sources.supports: AI agent that imports bills of materials from Excel

companies.body:
## What it does
Calculates the environmental impact of buildings and products across their
life, produces environmental product declarations (EPDs), and supports
regulatory and certification reporting, with large libraries of material data.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
Carbon is becoming a design constraint like cost. A firm that can compare
options on carbon automatically, from its models, has an advantage in bids
with carbon targets.

## Evidence and caveats
- Usage claims (150+ countries) are the company's own.

companies.name: OpenSpace
companies.summary: 360° site capture that automatically maps photos onto plans, with AI analytics and (since 2025) Disperse's progress tracking.
companies.ring_note: Reality capture is one of the more mature AI categories. Strong candidate for a standard site tool; compare with Buildots on a live project.

sources.title: OpenSpace company profile
sources.supports: San Francisco base; founders Jeevan Kalanithi, Michael Fleischman and Philip DeCamp; founded 2017

sources.title: OpenSpace announces new strategic partnerships to help bring Street View to construction
sources.supports: helmet-mounted capture; AI maps images onto plans without manual pinning

companies.body:
## What it does
A camera on a hard hat records a site walk; OpenSpace's AI places each image
on the floor plan automatically, building a time-stamped visual record of the
site that teams can browse like Street View. In October 2025 it bought
Disperse, a progress-tracking company (reported in search results; the
acquisition announcement itself wasn't read in this pass).

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
A complete visual history of every project is a foundation for later AI uses
(progress, quality, claims, training data), and capturing it costs little site
time.

## Evidence and caveats
- Funding totals vary widely between databases ($111m to $200m), so none is
  given here.
- The Disperse acquisition needs a primary source.

## To check
- Primary source for the Disperse acquisition; how many large contractors use it.

companies.name: Procore
companies.summary: A leading construction project-management platform, now adding AI agents through its "Helix" intelligence layer.
companies.ring_note: The platform is a mainstream choice for contractors. Its AI agents are newer (Agent Builder launched October 2025) and would be "trial" on their own; Procore says agents never act without sign-off.

sources.title: Procore advances the future of construction with new AI innovations at Groundbreak 2025
sources.supports: Agent Builder (October 2025) for no-code agents such as RFI drafting and daily logs; quote from Mortenson's Director of AI

sources.title: New Procore AI experience embeds Datagrid into Procore
sources.supports: 2026 "digital coworker" agents that act inside Procore (Deep Search, Submittal Reviewer, RFI, Contract Review, Daily Log)

sources.title: Procore Helix
sources.supports: Helix described as AI, agentic workflows, analytics and insights

companies.body:
## What it does
Cloud software for running construction projects: documents, drawings, RFIs,
submittals, budgets, daily logs and more. "Helix" is its AI layer: an
assistant, pre-built agents, and Agent Builder for firms to make their own.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
If a firm's project data already lives in Procore, its AI features can work
across that data without extra integration. The strategic question is whether
to build the firm's AI on a platform's agents (fast, but tied to that vendor)
or on its own data layer (more control, more work).

## Evidence and caveats
- Agent names and plan tiers changed between 2025 and 2026 announcements;
  check current documentation before quoting them.
- Headquarters and founding year not checked in this pass.

companies.name: TestFit
companies.summary: Generative design software that produces and tests building and site layouts for feasibility studies in minutes.
companies.ring_note: Established with developers, architects and contractors for early feasibility. Quick to trial on a live bid or site appraisal.

sources.title: TestFit lands $20M to expand real estate feasibility analytics software
sources.supports: $20m Series A (July 2022), total $22m

sources.title: Dallas' TestFit to launch generative design tool for building site planning
sources.supports: Dallas company; generative design tool launched July 2020; co-founders Clifton Harness (CEO) and Ryan Griege (CTO)

companies.body:
## What it does
Users set a site, building type and targets (units, parking, cost), and the
software generates and scores many layout options, including multi-site
studies.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
Moves early design from days of drawing to minutes of comparing, so a
design-and-build contractor can test more opportunities and price them
sooner.

## Evidence and caveats
- Founding year 2017 is from a 2021 Dallas Innovates piece (another report
  says code started in 2016). No funding after 2022 found.

companies.name: Togal.AI
companies.summary: AI take-off software that detects and measures spaces and features on drawings for estimators.
companies.ring_note: A focused tool with a clear payback test: run it on past bids and compare with the estimators' take-offs.

companies.body:
## What it does
Upload a set of drawings and the software finds and measures rooms, walls and
other elements automatically, producing quantities for estimators to check and
price.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
Estimating decides what a firm wins and whether it makes money. Faster take-off
lets the same team bid more work or spend time on judgement. It's also an easy
place to measure AI's value: compare against past jobs.

## Evidence and caveats
- Speed and accuracy claims vary by source (80% faster; 97% accuracy; up to
  90% less time) and all trace back to the company.

## To check
- Independent accuracy tests; coverage of UK drawing conventions.

companies.name: Trunk Tools
companies.summary: AI agents that read a project's documents (drawings, specs, RFIs, submittals) to answer questions and check work.
companies.ring_note: One of the most "agentic" products in construction, with big-contractor names attached, but young and fast-changing. Worth a close look for an AI-native strategy; evidence of outcomes is still mainly the company's own.

companies.body:
## What it does
Builds a connected map of a project's documents and runs AI agents on top:
answering site questions from the documents, checking submittals against the
spec, spotting changes between drawing revisions, and helping with RFIs and
contracts. It integrates with Autodesk Forma.

## Why it matters for an AI-native firm
This is close to what "AI at the centre" looks like day to day: every project
document is searchable and checked automatically, and agents do first drafts
of routine work for people to approve.

## Evidence and caveats
- Growth figures (5× revenue in six months; 1,000 projects) are the
  company's own claims.
- Headquarters not checked in this pass.

## To check
- Headquarters; how answers are cited and checked; data security terms.

analyses.title: The prefab and modular graveyard: why industrialized construction has failed
analyses.independence: Opinion newsletter; author's interests not checked
analyses.body:
**What it argues (from a search summary; not read in full):** first-
generation modular firms failed not because industrialisation is impossible
but because their models didn't fit construction's economic, operational and
financial realities.

**Useful for:** a counter-view to vendor optimism about offsite construction.

**Caveats:** opinion, not research. Read in full before citing.

analyses.title: Top 50 Contech startups of 2025
analyses.independence: Corporate venture arm of Cemex (a building-materials company); it invests in some of the startups it ranks
analyses.body:
**What it is:** an annual ranking (the sixth edition in 2025) of construction
tech startups, in four areas: Green Construction, Enhanced Productivity,
Construction Supply Chain and Future of Construction.

**Headline data quoted with it:** Contech investment in 2024 of about
$3.1 billion across 325 deals; deal count up about 38% but money up only about
2.3% on 2023; Enhanced Productivity 47% of deals, Green Construction 24%.

**Useful for:** finding startups to add to this radar, especially in Europe
and Latin America.

**Caveats:** the full list wasn't read in this pass. Cemex Ventures is an
investor, not a neutral judge.

analyses.title: AI powers $3.96B venture boom in US construction tech (BuiltWorlds Q2 2025 data)
analyses.independence: Trade press reporting an industry network's venture data
analyses.body:
**What it says:** in Q2 2025, $3.96 billion went into built-environment tech
startups; of 159 AEC deals, 110 involved AI/ML companies, which took about
$2.71 billion (about 68%).

**Useful for:** evidence that investment is now concentrated in AI, which
matters when judging which categories will keep improving fastest.

**Caveats:** different trackers disagree. Cemex Ventures put AI's share of
2025 contech funding at 77%; Superscout put it near two-thirds. Definitions of
"AI company" and "contech" differ, so compare trends, not exact numbers.

analyses.title: From start-up to scale-up: Accelerating growth in construction technology
analyses.independence: Consultancy research (independent of vendors, but McKinsey sells advice on this topic)
analyses.body:
**What it says (from summaries; the full PDF wasn't read in this pass):**
AEC is a roughly $12 trillion industry that has been slow to digitise.
Investment in AEC tech reached $50 billion between 2020 and 2022. The authors
mapped more than 3,000 AEC tech companies and expect consolidation to
continue. Demand for infrastructure, labour shortages and pressure for data
transparency are driving adoption.

**Useful for:** the scale-of-market framing and the argument that integration
and consolidation will decide which tools survive.

**Caveats:** written before the 2024–26 wave of generative AI and agents.
Figures like "talent investment raises the odds of digital success 2.5×" come
from a secondary summary (BDC Network) and should be checked in the PDF.

analyses.title: Foundamental (construction-tech venture firm) and the "data layer" argument
analyses.publisher: TechCrunch (fund announcement) and VC Sheet (partner profile)
analyses.independence: Venture investor; argues for the kinds of companies it backs
analyses.body:
**Why it's here:** Foundamental is a specialist construction-tech venture
firm (its newer fund targeted $85m for early-stage startups). One of its
partners, Shub Bhattacharya, argues that lasting value in construction AI will
come from data infrastructure and systems of record rather than thin AI-only
apps (per his VC Sheet profile: https://www.vcsheet.com/who/shub-bhattacharya).

**Useful for:** the central strategic question for an AI-native firm: own the
data layer, or rent AI features from platforms?

**Caveats:** the argument is summarised from a profile page, not a published
report; find a primary piece by the author before quoting.

analyses.title: What does Katerra's demise mean for the contech and modular industries?
analyses.body:
**Why it's here:** the leading cautionary tale for any plan to transform a
construction business through technology and vertical integration. See the
Katerra entry for a summary of causes and the other sources.

**Useful for:** pressure-testing a client's transformation plan: is it staged,
does each stage pay back, and is the core project economics sound?
